scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tambourin de Provence is a deep, two-headed drum of Arabic origin, mentioned as early as the 1080s and noted as the 'tabor' in the Chanson de Roland.
It became a staple of Provençal music and was later popularized in 18th-century European opera and keyboard suites by composers like Jean-Philippe Rameau, Handel, and Gluck.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The tambourin is associated with Provençal traditions, street parades (cercaviles), and festive events.
In Catalonia, the smaller tamborí is used in cobla ensembles for the sardana dance.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instruments are the tambourin de Provence (a deep, two-headed tenor drum) and the galoubet (a small, three-holed flute).
The tambourinaire plays both simultaneously, wearing the drum on a strap from the left arm and striking it with a wooden beater (massette) held in the right hand.
Listen for the tambourin de Provence, galoubet.
The pulse is duple meter.
A driving, rhythmic sound characterized by the steady, low-pitched pulse of a deep drum accompanied by the high-pitched, piercing melody of a three-holed flute.
